content: Evidence regarding the benefits of using admission tests other than cardiotocography (CTG) to prevent adverse perinatal outcomes during labor has not been firmly established. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of such alternative admission tests in reducing adverse perinatal outcomes. A systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register up to March 31, 2011. The study included randomized controlled trials (both individual and cluster) that compared the use of admission tests other than CTG for the prevention of adverse perinatal outcomes. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility and quality of the studies and extracted the relevant data. Only one study, involving 883 women, met the inclusion criteria. This study compared the use of sonographic assessment of the amniotic fluid index (AFI) upon admission to labor versus no sonographic assessment of AFI. The findings were as follows: 1. The rate of cesarean sections performed for fetal distress was significantly higher in the group that underwent sonographic AFI assessment (29 out of 447 women) compared to the control group (14 out of 436 women). The calculated risk ratio (RR) was 2.02, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 1.08 to 3.77. 2. The incidence of a low Apgar score (less than seven) at five minutes was not significantly different between the intervention group (10 out of 447 women) and the control group (7 out of 436 women). The RR was 1.39, with a 95% CI of 0.54 to 3.63. 3. The use of artificial oxytocin to augment labor was significantly higher in the intervention group (213 out of 447 women) compared to the control group (132 out of 436 women). The RR was 1.57, with a 95% CI of 1.32 to 1.87. 4. The rate of neonatal admissions to the NICU was not significantly different between the intervention group (35 out of 447 neonates) and the control group (33 out of 436 neonates). The RR was 1.03, with a 95% CI of 0.66 to 1.63. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of admission tests other than cardiotocography for fetal assessment during labor. They emphasized the need for well-designed randomized controlled trials with adequate sample sizes to evaluate the effectiveness of these alternative admission tests.
